name: Bilal Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. How does a normal working day go?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Tessler Auto Parts, brake pads, filters, batteries, wiper blades, for about four hundred garages around the region. First thing I look at the stock alerts, then I write to suppliers in Poland and Turkey, and sometimes I run the emails through a chatbot to tidy the English. The afternoons are quotes and chasing late lorries. I came across from the counter team three years ago, so I'm still learning, and Mo, the senior buyer, backs me up when it gets complicated.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Freja is a dental hygienist, full time, and we've got Oskar, twelve, and Yasmin, nine. We live in Eastwick, in a house with a mortgage we pay off steadily, and we keep more than six months of costs in savings. I cook on weekdays and Freja takes the weekends. Gareth Lund, who runs Tessler, is fair but watches every cent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, there's a lot of noise and not much to show. At work I'd say keep using the tools where they help and don't make a fuss. To friends I'd say AI is another tool, like the barcode scanner was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my bigger worry is the shift to electric cars. Fewer brake pads and no oil filters, and that hits our core parts. AI doesn't change that in the plateau world, but the shrinking of parts demand is already making Gareth look hard at costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and use the chatbot a bit more for emails and supplier summaries. I'd ask Mo to teach me how he forecasts electric-car parts, because that's where the future is. We'd keep saving about 300 a month, since Freja's work and ours are steady but I'd like extra cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled. Not thrilled, not worried, just a normal level of mortgage-and-school-fees concern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the electric cars shift. Is that already on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now the chatbot saves me maybe two hours a week. If it kept improving a bit it'd still need a person who knows a Peugeot from a Passat. That part of the job isn't going anywhere soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the chatbot you use would matter more if AI kept developing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. I know suppliers who still send me prices as PDF scans, and the tool can't read half of them. In the plateau world those little frictions stay, and I'm the one who sorts them.

say: I'd say there's a lot of noise and not much to show, and AI is another **tool**, like the barcode scanner was.
At work I'd say use it where it helps and don't make a **fuss**.
think: My bigger worry is the shift to **electric** cars, which cuts demand for brake pads and oil filters.
Gareth is already looking hard at **costs**, even with AI standing still.
do: Use the chatbot a bit more for supplier **emails** and summaries.
Ask Mo to teach me how he forecasts **electric-car** parts.
Keep saving **300** a month for extra cover.
feel: Pretty **settled**, with a normal level of mortgage and school-fees concern.
S0.quote: I know suppliers who still send me prices as PDF scans, and the tool can't read half of them.
fieldNote: His pressure is the electric-car shift in his firm's product line, not AI.
Already a light user, so a quiet AI world changes little.

steps.text: Use the chatbot more for supplier emails and summaries

Save 300 a month for extra cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, show me the proof, and meanwhile let's get ready. At work I'd say we should pick one or two jobs to try the software on and compare the results. To friends I'd say it's a big change but not the end of the world, and people should keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my kind of job is in the firing line. Reorder lists, price checks, emails to suppliers and chasing deliveries are most of the junior buyer's day. I use the chatbot for a few of those, and if I can do it with a chatbot, so can the firm, with fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a short course on automotive parts data and supply chains. I'd offer to run a trial of the AI forecasting tool for the brake range, to be the person who knows it. I'd save 450 a month instead of 300, and I'd tell Freja we'd not take on any new big costs for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. I can see the problem and I think I have a decent way to deal with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks do you think would be handed to software at Tessler first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The forecasting, the reordering, the email chasing and comparing prices. What stays is knowing which garage owner is in trouble and who's worth a favour, plus the odd odd-ball part nobody has in stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Gareth decide who stays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd look at who costs more and who's more useful. I'm cheaper than Mo but newer, so I'd need to show I can handle the tools. If he asked me to help pick the system, I'd take that as a good sign.

say: I'd say show me the proof, and meanwhile let's pick one or two **jobs** to try the software on and compare.
To friends I'd say it's a big change but people should keep **learning**.
think: My kind of job is in the firing line, since reorder lists, price checks and **supplier** emails are most of the day.
If I can do it with a chatbot, so can the firm, with **fewer** of us.

Offer to run the AI forecasting **trial** for the brake range.

S1.quote: If I can do it with a chatbot, so can the firm, with fewer of us.
fieldNote: Draws a straight line from his own chatbot use to the firm's possible cuts.
Responds by becoming the person who **runs the trial**, typical of a steady adapter.
Judges Gareth as fair but cost-driven.

steps.text: Take a short course in automotive parts data and supply chains
Offer to run the AI forecasting trial for the brake range

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready and we should be honest about that. At work I'd say let's not pretend, let's find out which of us has a role in two years. To friends I'd say we need a steady safety net and some kind of retraining right now, not in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My buying desk is basically gone by 2028. The software buys better, faster and without holidays. The garages and the delivery vans are hands-on, so they have until about 2031, which makes me think my future might be nearer the garage side than the screen side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Gareth in the first month and ask what Tessler's plan is. I'd look at roles that touch garages and customers, like account manager, because those are about relationships. I'd keep our spending lean for two years, save about 700 a month, and Freja and I would talk about whether she could take extra shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quite strongly. It's a short runway and I've got kids to feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the two years do to your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots that can change a gearbox in 2031 are a long way off, I think, so garages keep running for a few more years. But fewer cars come in with simple repairs, and that's another squeeze. I'd rather be the person the garage owners ring than the screen the head office uses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you picture the garages themselves in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years takes away my chance to learn gradually. I'd have to jump quickly, maybe into account management, and learn the rest on the job. I'm steady, not fast, so it'd feel like running with a heavy coat on.

say: I'd say nobody's ready and we should be honest about it, and we need a **safety** net now, not in five years.
At work I'd say let's find out which of us has a role in **two** years.
think: My buying desk is basically **gone** by 2028, because the software buys better and faster.
Garages and delivery vans are hands-on, so they last until about **2031**, which points me toward garage-side work.
do: Ask Gareth in the first **month** what Tessler's plan is.
Look at **account** manager roles that deal with garage owners.
Save about **700** a month and ask Freja about extra shifts.
feel: **Anxious**, quite strongly, because it's a short runway and I have kids to feed.
S2.quote: I'd rather be the person the garage owners ring than the screen the head office uses.
fieldNote: Sees the thinking-first, hands-on-later split and aims himself at the hands-on end, the garage owners.
Steady rather than fast, hence the 'heavy coat' image.
Spends the **cushion's** time on a switch to account work.

steps.text: Ask Gareth in month one what Tessler's plan is
Apply for account manager roles that work with garage owners
Ask Freja about taking extra dental shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people time if they use it, so let's start now. At work I'd suggest a plan for each role and a rule that people get notice. I'd say to friends the government should fund retraining before the big layoffs, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is workable. I think I'd have done a year or two of learning and moved into account management by the time AGI shows up. Seeing it coming lets me line up a role in advance, and that's worth a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd take a part-time course in business management at the evening college, and ask Gareth to let me shadow the account team. I'd save 500 a month and put some into a low-cost index fund as well. And I'd keep using the chatbot for emails so I don't fall behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anxious. There's a plan, and the plan has steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Is that a better deal than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On day one I'd just have a proper chat with Mo and Gareth, ask what roles will still be around. I'd write it down, make it a plan, put dates on it. I like a plan, it stops me worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently on day one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, yes. Two years is a sprint, five is a decent jog. I'd keep going to the football on Saturdays and wouldn't feel the walls closing in.

The government should fund **retraining** before the big layoffs, not after.

Seeing it coming lets me line up a **role** in advance.

S3.quote: Two years is a sprint, five is a decent jog.
fieldNote: Time lets him follow his natural style: plan, write it down, put dates on it.
Combines learning with a visible **shadowing** step inside the firm.

steps.text: Take an evening college course in business management

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people stay curious. At work I'd say let's build skills each year, not at the last minute. To friends I'd say good, let's just make sure it's fair when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fifty-three, the kids at university or close, and the mortgage nearly gone. Ten years feels like enough to move into something that lasts, like customer-facing work, or even train as a mechanic's service adviser. I wouldn't be happy to see my current job go, but it would be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue as a buyer for a while, use the tools more, and add skills yearly. I'd save for the kids' education, and put a chunk into pension and shares. In year three or four I'd move into account management, so I'm not stuck when the buying desk is automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's something to plan around, not lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years feel too far away to worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. It's easy to think there's loads of time and then wake up with two years left. So I'd pencil in checkpoints, like a review every spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell Oskar and Yasmin about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn how things work, and be good with people. A machine can do the paperwork, but someone has to talk to a worried customer. I'd tell them that adults change jobs several times, so don't hang your identity on one.

I'd say let's make sure it's **fair** when it comes.

I wouldn't be happy to see my current job go, but it would be **okay**.

Save for the kids' education and put a **chunk** into pension and shares.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, simply because I can't learn gradually. What would help is notice from Gareth, a paid course, and a safety net while people switch. Freja's job helps a lot too, and so does our savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like people to remember the middle, those of us who are not rich, not poor, and not tech people. We'll adapt if we're given time and a fair go.

headlineQuote: We'll adapt if we're given time and a fair go.
portrait: Bilal is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at Tessler Auto Parts, supplying brake pads, filters and batteries to about 400 garages.
He uses a chatbot **now and then** for supplier emails, and learns new tools once they're proven.
He and Freja, a dental hygienist, have two children, a mortgage and more than six months of savings.
He expects his buying desk to go and aims at **account management**, the relationship side of the business.
He plans in steps, with dates and checkpoints, and worries most when there's **no runway**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, because he can't learn gradually.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice** from Gareth, a paid course, and a safety net while people switch.
